Monday. Deepika finished her practice speech for the inter-school debate and looked at her brother. Jatin clapped. "Brilliant. Don't change a word." She went to bed smiling.
Saturday, two weeks later. The results went up on the notice board: Deepika was out in the first round. The judge's sheet said her points repeated and her rebuttal was missing. She read it three times, her ears hot. Brilliant? Then what was this?
Sunday. She put the sheet on Jatin's desk. "Did you actually think it was good?" He rubbed his neck. "I didn't want to discourage you." Deepika sat down on his bed. "Next time, tell me one thing that's weak. Otherwise your 'brilliant' doesn't tell me anything." He nodded and picked up a pen.

qa.q: What did the judge's sheet say about Deepika's speech?
qa.a: The judge's sheet said her points repeated and her rebuttal was missing.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel when she read the results, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt confused and embarrassed; she read the sheet three times with hot ears and wondered what Jatin's "brilliant" had meant.

qa.q: What did Deepika ask Jatin to do next time, and why is it a wise request?
qa.a: She asked him to name one weak thing, because honest feedback is what makes his praise believable and useful.

qa.q: Why might Jatin have said "Brilliant" on Monday?
qa.a: He cared about his sister and did not want to discourage her, so he chose comfort over honest feedback.

grounding: A teenager feels warm at her brother's constant praise, then confused when results disagree, showing that praise that is never calibrated stops being useful.

passage:
Come, Madhuri, sit with your Dada. You asked why I always tell you exactly which bars you played badly. When I was fifteen, I took tabla lessons from a teacher everyone loved. Whatever I played, he said, "Wah, Vishal, first class!" I floated home every Thursday.
Then came the grade exam. The examiner stopped me halfway and said my rhythm kept slipping. I sat on the bus afterwards completely lost. Had my teacher been fooling me for a whole year?
The next week I went back and asked him straight out. He looked ashamed and said he hadn't wanted me to lose interest. From then on I asked him every single week for one mistake to fix. That is when I actually started to improve.

qa.q: What did the examiner say about Vishal's playing?
qa.a: The examiner said his rhythm kept slipping.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling on the bus after the exam?
qa.a: He felt completely lost and confused, wondering whether his teacher had been fooling him for a whole year.

qa.q: What choice did Vishal make after talking to his teacher, and how did it help?
qa.a: He began asking every week for one mistake to fix, and that is when he actually started to improve.

qa.q: Why might the tabla teacher have kept saying "first class"?
qa.a: He didn't want Vishal to lose interest, so he gave constant praise, and he later looked ashamed when he saw what it had cost.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a teenager, a teacher's constant praise felt good until an exam showed otherwise, and uncalibrated praise stopped meaning anything.

passage:
Monday. Hrithik came back from the under-16 trial match with 4 runs off 30 balls. He had edged two, missed three, and been bowled trying a wild swing. At home, his older brother Irfan ruffled his hair. "Superb, yaar. You looked like a proper opener." Hrithik grinned and slept well.
Saturday. The selection list went up on the club board. His name wasn't there. He read it three times. "But everyone said I was batting well," he told Irfan, confused. Irfan looked at the floor.
The next Wednesday, after nets, Hrithik sat beside his brother on the steps. "Bhaiya, you watched every ball. Tell me the truth. What went wrong?"
Irfan took a breath. "Your feet don't move to the short ones. You swing at everything outside off."
It stung. But for the first time in weeks, Hrithik knew what to practise.

qa.q: How many runs did Hrithik score in the trial match?
qa.a: He scored 4 runs off 30 balls.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when he read the selection list?
qa.a: He felt confused and let down, because everyone had said he was batting well, so the missing name made no sense to him.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Hrithik, and why?
qa.a: Asking Irfan directly for the truth worked, because a specific note about his feet and wild swings gave him something real to practise.

qa.q: Why might Irfan have said "superb" after the trial?
qa.a: Irfan probably wanted to protect his younger brother's mood, but his looking at the floor later shows he knows the praise did not help.

grounding: It shows a teenager feeling good about empty praise after a weak performance, then confused by the result, and finally asking for honest feedback.

passage:
Himani, come, sit. You want to know why your Aparna Mausi never sang on the radio? I'll tell you.
When I was fifteen, everyone on our lane said I sang like a nightingale. My father clapped at every little function. My aunts cried at every bhajan. Nobody ever said I rushed the high notes, or that my breath ran out before the end of a line. So I believed I was ready.
The radio station held an audition. I went in my best sari, full of pride. Halfway through, the man at the desk lifted his hand and said, "Thank you. Your breathing needs work." That was all.
I cried all the way home. I wasn't angry at him. I was confused, and then angry at everyone who had only ever clapped. Much later, my music teacher gave me the truth, kindly, one note at a time. That, Himani, is what helped.

qa.q: What did the man at the audition say about Aparna's singing?
qa.a: He said, "Thank you. Your breathing needs work."

qa.q: How did young Aparna feel on the way home from the audition?
qa.a: She felt confused and hurt, and then angry at everyone who had only ever clapped, because their praise had left her unprepared.

qa.q: At which turning point in the story did things start to improve for Aparna?
qa.a: Things improved when her music teacher gave her the truth kindly, one note at a time, so she finally had something to work on.

qa.q: How might Aparna's father have seen his clapping at every function?
qa.a: He probably saw it as love and encouragement, without realising it hid the rushed high notes and short breath she needed to fix.

grounding: An aunt tells how constant praise as a teenager felt warm but left her confused after a failed audition, and how honest teaching helped.

passage:
The art school portfolio had to be uploaded by nine that night, and the cyber café near the bus depot shut at eight. Manjula had forty minutes.
All month, her cousin Deepak had flipped through her sketches and said, "Masterpiece. Masterpiece. This one too." Her parents said the same. So when the art teacher's mock review came back that morning with 4 out of 10 and "proportions weak, hands unfinished," Manjula stared at the paper, lost. Which was true?
She held out the file. "Deepak, just pick the two weakest. Quickly."
"They're all good, yaar."
"Please. I don't have time for good."
He hesitated, then pointed at the girl on the stairs and the market scene. "Maybe these. The hands look... stiff."
Manjula swapped them for two older drawings, scanned the rest, and ran. At 7:52 the upload bar turned green.

qa.q: What score did the art teacher's mock review give?
qa.a: It gave 4 out of 10, with "proportions weak, hands unfinished."

qa.q: How did Manjula feel when she read the mock review?
qa.a: She felt lost and confused, because a month of "masterpiece" from Deepak and her parents clashed with the teacher's low score.

qa.q: What worked when time was short?
qa.a: Asking Deepak to pick the two weakest drawings worked, because a specific honest answer let her swap them before the upload deadline.

qa.q: What is it like for Deepak when Manjula asks for the weakest drawings?
qa.a: It is uncomfortable for him, because he is used to saying everything is good, but he realises honest help is what she needs.

grounding: It shows a teenager warmed by constant praise, then confused by a weak review, learning that uncalibrated praise is not usable information.

passage:
After the inter-school dance competition in Kochi, Elizabeth came off stage breathless. She had missed two counts and nearly slipped in the turn.
Her friend Kashish hugged her. "You were amazing! Best in the whole show!"
Her mother said the same. So did her aunt on the phone. Elizabeth let herself believe it. That night she replayed the compliments, warm and happy.
The next day the results went up on the school noticeboard. Elizabeth was eleventh out of twelve.
She stood there, cheeks burning. Had everyone been lying? Or had they just not been watching?
At lunch she asked Kashish, "Did I really look good?"
Kashish hesitated. "I mean... you tried really hard."
Elizabeth nodded slowly. "Next time, can you tell me what went wrong? Otherwise I don't know what to fix."

qa.q: Where did Elizabeth place in the results?
qa.a: Eleventh out of twelve.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when she saw the results?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt embarrassed and confused, cheeks burning, wondering whether everyone had been lying.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth ask Kashish for, and why does it help?
qa.a: Honest feedback next time about what went wrong, so praise becomes information she can actually use.

qa.q: Why might Kashish have said 'You were amazing'?
qa.a: Kashish likely wanted to comfort her friend in the moment, not realising it would leave Elizabeth confused later.

grounding: Shows a teenager warmed by praise for a weak performance, then confused by the results, learning that uncalibrated praise is not usable.
